abstract: Utilizing abundant feldspar (FS) as a precursor supports the economic feasibility of alkali-activated binders (AABs). However, the material's inherent low reactivity results in suboptimal mechanical properties, restricting its use in structural concrete. This paper addresses this drawback by developing a high-strength binder incorporating high-volume FS as a partial replacement for artificial slag (AS). The superior reactivity of AS was found to compensate for the strength loss resulting from the poor reactivity of FS. Moreover, incorporating FS results in a reduction in water demand and an increase in the alkali concentration relative to AS. Sodium silicate-activated AS mortar (at a constant Na 2 Oeq of 5 wt%) recorded 1-d and 120-d compressive strengths of 91 MPa and 116 MPa, respectively. Although replacing AS with high-volume FS results in a compressive strength reduction, the mortar with 70 vol% FS still achieved a high 120-d compressive strength of 91 MPa. The filling effect is the predominant mechanism of FS within the formulated alkali-activated system, as determined by various microstructural analyses. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations further support this interpretation by indicating a relatively weak interaction between FS and the alkali activator. In contrast, limestone powder (LP), considered as an alternative substitute for AS, exhibits a stronger interaction tendency, consistent with chemical expectations. However, the FS-based mortar showed a 10% higher 120-d strength. The proposed strategy not only achieves the production of high-strength mortar but also paves the way for global standardization of alkali-activated binders by incorporating AS and FS with consistent physical and chemical performance.

title: Microstructure and mechanical properties of lignocellulosic magnesium potassium phosphate cement composites modified with activated biochar
abstract: ABSTRACT Magnesium potassium phosphate cement (MKPC) is a rapid-hardening binder suitable for ambient-temperature fabrication of lignocellulosic composites. This study investigates potassium hydroxide (KOH)-activated wood biochar as a matrix-scale modifier in MKPC composites reinforced with wood particles or coir fibres. Wood biochar was activated at 400 °C for 1 or 2 h and used to replace 5 wt.% of the MgO–KH 2 PO 4 binder fraction, while wood particles or coir fibres were incorporated at 10 or 15 wt.% of the dry binder mass. KOH activation increased oxygen-containing surface functionalities and micro-/mesopore development relative to pristine biochar, while milling reduced particle-size differences among the biochar variants. At the binder scale, biochar incorporation modified early-age heat-flow response without substantially changing cumulative heat release. Phase and thermal analyses confirmed struvite-K as the dominant crystalline reaction product, while mercury intrusion porosimetry indicated redistribution of accessible pore-throat sizes toward finer entry radii. Elemental mapping showed increased spatial association between carbon-rich biochar domains and K–P-rich phosphate reaction products in the activated systems. At the composite scale, reinforcement architecture controlled mechanical behaviour, with coir-fibre composites exhibiting higher flexural strength and toughness than wood-particle composites. Activated biochar produced additional matrix-scale improvements in flexural performance, while recovery of internal bond strength was consistent with matrix strengthening rather than direct modification of the reinforcement–matrix interface. Water absorption was governed mainly by the reinforcement type and loading, whereas the change in thickness remained below 1% after 72 h of immersion.

Strain rate dependent performance of graphene-reinforced concrete: An experimental study
abstract: ABSTRACT Graphene has been extensively studied due to its unique and exceptional combination of properties that promise revolutionary applications across many fields. While graphene has demonstrated its promise in improving the mechanical properties of concrete under quasi-static loading, the research on its effectiveness under dynamic loading is limited. This study addresses this gap by investigating the reinforcing effects of graphene on the mechanical behaviour of concrete under both quasi-static and dynamic loadings. Different graphene contents were added to the concrete mixes to assess their impact on compressive, splitting tensile, and flexural strengths of concrete. Quasi-static tests were conducted using a universal testing machine, while dynamic tests were carried out using a split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) and a drop-weight hammer. The results revealed that the addition of 0.1% graphene to the concrete significantly enhanced both the quasi-static and dynamic compressive, splitting tensile, and flexural strengths, as well as the flexural energy absorption. The strain rate effects were also characterised using the dynamic increase factor (DIF). Moreover, microstructural analysis using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive spectrometer (EDS), and mercury intrusion porosimeter (MIP) revealed the mechanisms of microstructural crack formation and propagation, providing insights into the macro-scale mechanical behaviour of graphene-reinforced concrete. The results highlight the potential of graphene to significantly enhance the mechanical properties of concrete under both quasi-static and high strain rate loadings, offering valuable implications for the design and construction of structures exposed to dynamic loading conditions.

A flexible cement-based supercapacitor with engineered pore structure for integrated multifunctional energy storage
abstract: Cement-based supercapacitors are emerging as key enablers of the green transition, unifying the widespread infrastructural presence of cement with the ability to store electrical energy. However, their inherent rigidity has hindered integration into irregular, free-form architectural surfaces. Here, we report the first flexible cement-based supercapacitor, which combines high electrochemical performance with exceptional mechanical adaptability. The device employs a cement-composite electrolyte engineered with a tailored network of mesopores and capillary pores, achieving an ionic conductivity of 35.28 mS cm −1 alongside a low Young's modulus of 81.6 MPa. In an asymmetric electrode configuration, the supercapacitor delivers an areal capacitance of 215.3 mF cm −2 , an energy density of 76.55 μWh cm −2 , and a power density of 726.95 μW cm −2 , with 83.3% capacitance retention over 2000 cycles. It operates reliably from −10 to 65 °C, withstands mechanical damage without failure, provides a 7 °C thermal insulation benefit, and shows negligible performance loss after six months outdoors. Capable of efficient solar energy storage, it can power small electronic devices such as LEDs, a mobile phone, and fans even when bent or twisted. This work demonstrates a versatile, deformable energy-storing cement, paving the way for multi-function building materials in next-generation free-form architecture.

Quantification of deformation and cracking processes of an aggregate due to alkali–silica reaction using digital volume correlation from X-ray CT images
abstract: : This study aims to provide insights into the location of expansion due to alkali–silica reaction (ASR) by quantifying deformations during the early stage of expansion of a single reactive andesite aggregate embedded within cement paste. One-month time-lapse microstructural information was obtained by performing global (low-resolution) and local (high-resolution) X-ray computed tomography (CT) on the specimens. High-resolution scans were used to measure displacement fields using mechanics-informed digital volume correlation (DVC). The CT images revealed the formation of cracks inside the aggregate along its surface after 14 days, followed by crack opening and propagation. The DVC results showed outward-directed displacements from the inner surface of the aggregate, indicating the presence of expansive sites on the surface, even when no crack was observed in the CT images. After cracking, large displacements developed in the direction perpendicular to the cracks. The mechanisms of ASR expansion pressure generation, which explain the observed deformation and crack changes, are discussed in relation to previous propositions.

title: Alkalinity-dependent carbonation of ground granulated blast-furnace slag: From glass dissolution to competitive precipitation
Multiscale carbon synergy in conductive cementitious composites: dimension-dependent construction of an axon-synapse-inspired conductive network
abstract: Understanding how multiscale carbon fillers construct conductive pathways in cementitious matrices remains critical for designing smart cement-based materials. Inspired by neural signal transmission, we develop a multiscale carbon synergy strategy to construct an axon-synapse-inspired conductive network within the cementitious matrix by integrating microscale carbon fibers (CF) with nanoscale carbon nanotubes (CNT) or graphene (G). In this bioinspired architecture, CF serves as the long-range conductive backbone, while CNT and G act as dimension-dependent local bridging units that connect adjacent fibers, pores, and microcracks, converting discrete contacts into a spatially redundant conductive network. A percolation threshold is identified at 0.4 vol% CF. On this basis, the lowest resistivity reaches 0.22 Ω·m at 0.2 wt% CNT and 0.21 Ω·m at 0.6 wt% G, together with improved thermal conductivity. Meanwhile, 0.4 wt% G provides the best mechanical synergy, increasing the 28-day compressive and flexural strengths by 16.95% and 14.29%, respectively. To interrogate this mechanism, freeze-thaw perturbation is employed as a controlled perturbation tool to modulate pore-water phase state and network topology. The results show that electrical response is governed by the coupling of ionic phase transition and electronic pathway evolution. Low-content systems undergo irreversible pathway rupture, whereas high-content systems exhibit partial network reconstruction; after 90 cycles, Rct decreases from 37.85 to 17.77 Ω in CNT0.5-CF0.4 and from 20.38 to 6.39 Ω in G1.0-CF0.4. This work establishes a mechanistic framework for dimension-dependent conductive network design in cementitious composites.

Electrodeposition to reduce the impact of cracks on steel corrosion in concrete
abstract: Electrodeposition has been proposed as a method to promote mineral precipitation in cracked reinforced concrete, potentially limiting ingress of aggressive agents and delaying corrosion initiation. However, the extent to which electrodeposition-induced crack filling improves corrosion resistance under marine exposure, and the influence of electrolyte composition on the effectiveness and mechanism of electrodeposition, remains overlooked. This study investigated deposition behaviour of electrodeposition in either artificial seawater or Ca-Mg nitrate solution and evaluated corrosion performance of electrodeposition-treated (2x3) and non-electrodeposition-treated (references, 2x2) specimens during artificial seawater exposure. Reinforced concrete cylinders containing tensile-induced transverse cracks underwent three-month electrodeposition treatment, followed by a three-month artificial seawater exposure. Crack filling and deposition patterns were examined using X-ray computed tomography (XCT), optical microscopy, and μXRF elemental mapping, while corrosion behaviour was assessed through half-cell potential monitoring and post-exposure CT. Analytical interpretation was further used to interpret observed electrodeposition behaviour. A difference in Ca 2+ and Mg 2+ ion concentrations between the Ca-Mg nitrate solution and artificial seawater results in different crack-filling behaviour. Electrodeposition in Ca-Mg nitrate solution resulted in extensive internal crack filling reaching the steel-concrete interface, independent of crack geometry and width (maximum surface crack width 0.75 mm), and no corrosion was observed. In contrast, electrodeposition treatment in artificial seawater resulted in deposits primarily near the crack mouth and an influence of crack geometry. In these specimens, corrosion was prevented in two specimens and reduced in the third. The findings demonstrate that electrodeposition can delay corrosion initiation in cracked concrete when sufficient internal crack filling is achieved.

Photovoltaic glass waste derived activators for one-part alkali-activated binders: Reaction mechanisms and phase evolution
abstract: One-part alkali-activated materials (AAMs) are increasingly promoted as low-CO 2 alternatives to Portland cement, yet their sustainability and commercial viability are constrained by the high energy demand, cost, and embodied carbon of conventional solid activators such as sodium metasilicate. While waste-derived activators have recently been proposed, the mechanistic links between the activator chemistry, dissolution behaviour, reaction kinetics, and the microstructure in one-part systems remain poorly understood. This study addresses this knowledge gap by valorising end-of-life photovoltaic (PV) glass as a source of sodium silicate powders synthesised via low-temperature alkaline fusion (250 °C), with the glass-to-NaOH ratio tuned to achieve silica modulus (M s ) of 1.0–1.5. These PV-glass-derived activators are systematically compared with commercial sodium metasilicate activators in one-part alkali-activated binders, focusing on dissolution behaviour, reaction kinetics, phase assemblage and microstructural evolution. The PV-glass-derived activators generate a higher proportion of depolymerised Q 0 silicate species and produce nanocrystalline C–S–H-type phases in the dissolution residues, which could accelerate early-age reactions through both seeding and chemical effects. Increasing M s reduces the dissolution efficiency and slows early-age reactions, lowering 1-day strength, yet 28-day compressive strengths remain comparable to those obtained with the commercial activator. Phase analysis reveals strätlingite formation in systems with lower-M s synthetic activators, while higher PV-glass contents (corresponding to higher M s value) promote denser microstructures and more cross-linked C–(N)–A–S–H networks. This work advances the fundamental understanding of waste-PV glass activation and outlines a scalable pathway to decarbonise one-part AAMs.

Impact resistance of novel 3D-printed concrete composite beams under drop-weight loading: Experimental and numerical investigation
abstract: Extrusion-based 3D concrete printing (3DCP) enables automated, formwork-free fabrication of cementitious components, but its structural use is still limited by quasi-brittle fracture, weak interlayer interfaces, and anisotropic damage evolution. This study develops and assesses an impact-resilient 3D-printed cementitious composite beam system based on two complementary mechanisms: an embedded steel–concrete composite reinforcement beam, where perforated steel plates and welded shear keys provide distributed mechanical interlock across printed layers, and a detachable deformation-triggered elastomeric constraint (EC) designed to engage mainly during the large-deflection stage. Drop-weight impact tests were conducted on 12 specimens using a 265 kg falling mass. Three configurations were examined: foamed benchmark beams, 3D-printed composite beams, and 3D-printed composite beams with EC. Two loading orientations relative to the printing axes and drop heights from 0.4 to 2.0 m were considered. Synchronised measurements of contact force, support reaction, deflection, strain, and damage evolution confirmed a two-stage impact response, consisting of an inertia-dominated force peak followed by a large-deflection damage stage. The EC did not systematically increase the initial peak impact force, but significantly improved post-peak force retention, rebound recovery, and damage tolerance. For matched cases with rebound, maximum and residual deflections were reduced by 16.7%–42.3% and 25.0%–53.2%, respectively. Under the most severe impact case, the baseline 3D-printed beam exhibited collapse-type behaviour, whereas the EC-enhanced beam remained rebound-capable. A validated Abaqus/Explicit model further showed that EC engagement stabilises the steel–concrete load-transfer path and mitigates late-stage interlayer damage, cementitious matrix degradation, and steel-plate instability.

Optimizing crack control and ductility in sustainable ultra-high performance concrete by using hybrid steel and UHMW-PE fibers and mineral fillers
abstract: While the ductility of tensile strain-hardening UHPFRC is critical for load-bearing capacity at the ultimate limit state and crack control under service conditions, recent studies reveal that conventional UHPFRC with 2–4% fiber volume often fails to achieve the recommended 5‰ tensile strain for tension-critical concrete structures. This paradox arises because increased ductility is frequently linked to larger microcrack widths, necessitating a carefully optimized solution. Building on advances in UHPFRC with hybrid stiff steel and flexible Ultra-High Molecular Weight Polyethylene (UHMW-PE) fibers, this work uniquely addresses both crack width reduction under service conditions and enhanced ductility. Significant portions of cement were replaced with recycled waste granite and limestone powders to promote sustainability. Several UHPFRC mix designs were developed, incorporating variations in fiber type (steel and UHMW-PE), length (6 mm and 13 mm), dosage (0–2% by volume), and hybrid configurations. For steel fibers, two distinct casting methods were employed. Tensile properties were assessed through bending tests combined with inverse analysis in accordance with Swiss SIA 2052 standards, while post-peak behavior was modeled using non-linear finite element analysis (NLFEA). Crack widths were measured using digital image correlation (DIC). Results showed that hybrid UHPFRC, combining stiff steel and ductile UHMW-PE fibers, demonstrated superior strain-hardening, reduced microcrack widths, enhanced ductility, and increased fracture energy while lowering the embodied carbon footprint. Microcracks were kept below 30 μm to ensure impermeability, and hardening strains exceeded 5‰ in tensile-controlled sections. The developed UHPFRC with hybrid fibers and mineral fillers offers a promising solution for advanced structural applications, balancing durability, cost-efficiency, and sustainability.

title: A systematic approach for material selection and printing parameter optimization in 3D lateral printing concrete
Characterizing buildability development of early-age 3D printed concrete using guided waves
abstract: Recent advancements in 3D printing of concrete (3DPC) have highlighted significant potential for formwork-free construction, geometric freedom, and reduced labor demand. However, ensuring buildability during layer-by-layer fabrication requires real-time control of fresh-state concrete properties, yet parameters that relate material behavior to structural buildability in 3DPC are still lacking. To address the need, this study explores an ultrasonic guided-wave technique for monitoring green strength development in 3DPC during fabrication across different mixture types. Ultrasonic and green strength tests were performed over the first 120 min after specimen fabrication. External waveguides, acrylic and aluminum plates equipped with two bonded PZT sensors, were mounted on one side of the specimens to monitor the leakage of ultrasonic energy from the plates into the concrete. Of the two waveguide materials, acrylic was more effective for monitoring green strength development at this very early age. As hydration-induced solidification progressed, the guided-wave parameter (normalized S0 guided-mode peak amplitude) decreased owing to increasing energy leakage into concrete, while the corresponding attenuation parameter increased, quantifying leakage-related energy loss. Strong correlations (R 2 higher than 0.93) between the ultrasonic parameters and green strength indicate that the guided-wave parameters can reliably capture early-age mechanical evolution relevant to buildability in 3DPC. Furthermore, the ultrasonic measurements demonstrated sensitivity to differences in early-age material development among the mixtures. An approach to use the developed ultrasonic parameters to estimate green strength development is proposed.
